messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Ravi was 32, a married South Asian man who had come to the United States to build a steadier life, and by the time he first described the robbery he was working long shifts as a housekeeper at a hotel near downtown. The attack had happened on his walk home after an evening shift, when the streets were thinning out and he was carrying the small amount of cash he had just been paid. He remembered the stranger stepping out from between two parked cars as if he had been waiting for him, the brief flash of fear when he realized there was nowhere easy to go, and the hard, humiliating moment when the man closed in, took what he wanted, and left him shaken on the sidewalk. Ravi did not describe the scene in dramatic language; instead, he spoke in short fragments, stopping and starting as if the story became stuck in his throat. He knew exactly what had happened, but when he tried to tell it in fuller detail, he said he could not find the words. The memory remained startlingly clear to him nonetheless, almost too clear, with the sharp layout of the street, the position of the cars, the look of the man’s face, and the sudden sense of being trapped all returning with an almost photographic quality.

In the weeks that followed, the robbery stayed close to him in an intimate, bodily way. When the memory came back, it did not feel like a distant recollection but like something happening again inside his body, and he would tense and press a hand to the same parts of himself that had hurt during the event. He said that the pain seemed to return in those places with the memory, as if his body recognized the attack before his mind had time to organize it. He was careful in the way he spoke about this, almost embarrassed by it, as though he feared it sounded impossible, but the pattern was consistent in his account: the recollection arrived with clear images and with physical discomfort that made him go still and wait for it to pass. He found himself especially unsettled when he was alone with the memory at night after work, lying in bed beside his wife and trying not to let his thoughts travel back to that street corner. At those moments, he could summon the scene in exact detail and yet still feel unable to put it into ordinary language, as if the event remained closer to sensation than to story.

Over time, Ravi’s view of other people changed in a way he described as deeply unsettling. Before the robbery, he had considered himself cautious but generally trusting, the kind of man who gave strangers the benefit of the doubt. Afterward, that felt naïve to him. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that a calm face or an ordinary jacket could hide someone dangerous, and that a person could be standing only a few feet away from you while intending to harm you. He said he now thought people could not be trusted, not in some abstract philosophical sense but in the concrete, daily sense of sharing a street, a hallway, or an elevator with someone whose intentions he could not know. Those beliefs were strongest when he was out in public, particularly on his way home from work, and they made the city feel different to him. The neighborhood that had once seemed merely busy now felt risky, and even a harmless passerby could make him scan their hands, their pace, and the space around them. What frightened him most was how ordinary danger now seemed to him; he said the world itself felt dangerous, not only the place where the robbery happened but everywhere he had to move through strangers.

This way of seeing others and the world altered the texture of his daily life. At work, where he moved through guest corridors, service elevators, and the lobby in uniform, he found himself watching the people around him more closely than before, especially men who moved quickly or approached from behind. He still did his job, but the hotel no longer felt neutral. Every unfamiliar face could seem like a possible threat, and every entrance or hallway reminded him that a person could appear suddenly and close the distance before he was ready. Outside work, he became more reluctant to linger on the street after dark, and he kept his route home as direct as possible. His wife noticed that he was quieter and more guarded, but Ravi struggled to explain what had changed because so much of it lived in the specific, wordless certainty that people could not be taken at face value and that danger could arrive when he was least prepared.

He sought help only after these experiences had become difficult to carry alongside work and marriage, and after several weeks of trying to manage them on his own. By then, the robbery still came back to him vividly, with bodily pain that made him freeze, and his distrust had become a constant part of how he moved through the world. He was most afraid that this would remain his new normal, that he would always have to live as though any stranger might be a threat, and he was most hoping that therapy might help him feel able to move through his job, his neighborhood, and his life with his wife without carrying the attack into every ordinary day.
